Sunday, May 31, 2026

Why so many Americans moved to the middle of nowhere

Places like Fulshear and Buckeye are more popular lately than New York City and Boston.

BY MARK DENT (https://x.com/mdent05?_hsenc=p2ANqtz-9T2_fqvsggw9W11El2Yg2HrGme0RLdFp8frtVIX-yiKhIwoRTSeOh8dPXCBESFajmD3VwtQXdIDgTIBZReJ9n_kQ89bA&_hsmi=421356992 )

If you’re in your 30s or 40s and having conversations with friends about where to buy homes, you might be hearing some strange names discussed.

- Buckeye, Arizona
- Fulshear, Texas
- Port Chester, New York
- Moncks Corner, South Carolina
- Centralia, Washington

They sound like they’re in the middle of nowhere. But they’re actually adding more residents than Los Angeles and New York City.

In May, the US Census Bureau released new data that highlighted the rapid growth of formerly sleepy towns and struggles for many big cities.

From 2020 to 2025, the 25 largest cities in the US grew by 1.3%, compared to 3.1% for the country as a whole.

Although about half of those cities saw average or above-average growth rates, many glamour cities, like New York City, Boston, and Los Angeles, declined in population. Dallas and Washington, DC, were basically flat.

The Hustle

Meanwhile, in the same time period, the 25 fastest-growing cities with at least 20k population were nearly all exurbs on the fringes of metro areas that have seen cornfields and pastures turn into subdivisions and shopping centers.

And this isn’t just a case of smaller places naturally seeing a higher percentage growth over larger places given their size. Over the last year, exurbs like Fulshear and Celina, Texas, saw more numeric population growth than all but five of the 25 largest cities.

The Hustle

Until a decade or two ago, many of these places had populations of just a few thousand. They’re located as far as 50 miles from a city center.

How did so many Americans end up practically in the middle of nowhere? And how far outside of cities are they willing to go?

The 15-minute city vs the one-minute city

The simplest answer for this shift starts back in March 2020, at the onset of the COVID pandemic.

Basement interest rates, coupled with remote work offering the ability to spread out, triggered one of the wildest seller’s markets in recent history. The median home sales price in the US shot up by 35% from late 2019 to late 2022. (They’ve declined slightly since then.)

Before the pandemic, a city like Boston was already unaffordable for middle class residents. But with a median sales price at ~$661k (https://www.boston.gov/sites/default/files/file/2020/11/Sales%20Report%2C%202019.pdf?_hsenc=p2ANqtz-9T2_fqvsggw9W11El2Yg2HrGme0RLdFp8frtVIX-yiKhIwoRTSeOh8dPXCBESFajmD3VwtQXdIDgTIBZReJ9n_kQ89bA&_hsmi=421356992 ) , homes weren’t insurmountable for the upper middle class.

That’s no longer the case. Median home sales prices checked in at $849.6k this spring, according to Redfin, or $764 per square foot. Typical Boston houses are out of reach for all but a small number of residents, even in one of the wealthiest areas of the country.

Price relief comes farther out of the city. Worcester County, an hour’s drive west of Boston, featuring towns like Shrewsbury, has attracted would-be Boston residents.

The Hustle

But the shift to exurbs is also about a preference in lifestyle. Many Americans want larger homes than they can get in big cities.

Take Fulshear, Texas, for example. The city, ~40 minutes west of Houston, grew by nearly 300% from 2020 to 2025, from a population of 16.3k to 64.6k.

Houston has plenty of space and sprawl but still doesn’t compare to Fulshear, where the average house size is ~50% larger.

The Hustle

Richard Florida, a prominent urbanist and visiting distinguished professor at Vanderbilt University, has described (https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/whats-wrong-with-downtown-dallas/?_hsenc=p2ANqtz-9T2_fqvsggw9W11El2Yg2HrGme0RLdFp8frtVIX-yiKhIwoRTSeOh8dPXCBESFajmD3VwtQXdIDgTIBZReJ9n_kQ89bA&_hsmi=421356992 ) the urban-to-exurban shift as a preference between a 15-minute city and a one-minute city.

- The 15-minute city, a well-known concept among planners, involves living in a dense area where groceries, parks, restaurants, jobs, and schools are within 15 minutes by walking or public transit.
- The one-minute city is more about loading up on amenities at your house. As Florida explains, it involves living somewhere far-flung with “a gymnasium, a home theater, two offices, play spaces for my kids, a big backyard with outdoor space and a play structure, and maybe a pool.”

Many exurbs have master-planned communities (https://heartlandtexas.com/?_hsenc=p2ANqtz-9T2_fqvsggw9W11El2Yg2HrGme0RLdFp8frtVIX-yiKhIwoRTSeOh8dPXCBESFajmD3VwtQXdIDgTIBZReJ9n_kQ89bA&_hsmi=421356992 ) featuring multiple pools, walking trails, soccer fields, and fitness centers, giving them the spirit of a one-minute city.

There might not be a better example for portraying all these shifts than Dallas.

The city lost population from 2024 to 2025 and saw modest growth going back to 2020. The same was true with Dallas’s suburbs. But its exurbs, with more bang for the buck and open space, exploded in population, both from Texans seeking a change and out-of-state newcomers moving in.

The Hustle

Celina, way up north of Dallas, added 12.7k residents from 2024 to 2025. It was also the fastest-growing city in the country (for cities with at least 20k pop.) by percent change in that timeframe. Nearby Princeton, Melissa, Anna, Forney, and Greenville were in the top 15.

How long can this last?

There’s one big problem with America’s exurban boom: these cities might already be too popular.

            Hi, glorious human.

My left eyelid has been twitching for the past month or so.

It's a quick, intermittent fluttering, like my eyelid is trying to send me distress signals in Morse code.

"We haven't been getting enough sleep," my eyelid taps out.

"ABORT. We are sTreSS*d," it taps.

"You are currently 97% coffee," it warns. "R U ok?"

Which is my way of explaining my absence here these past few weeks: I have been heads down and frantically grasping every moment I have to finish up the final draft of this infuriating my delightful new book.

A few weeks ago I found out that its deadline was not—"I repeat NOT," Eye Twitch shouts—the end of June, as sweet, clueless me had been thinking back in April when I was happy and young and innocent.

Instead, the deadline was cold-splash-of-water-May 15. A full 40 days and 40 nights earlier than I expected.

You can do a lot in 40 days and 40 nights.

You can survive a flood in Noah's Ark. Wait for Moses to come down from Mount Sinai. Endure a quarantine. Procrastinate doing actual work by researching how the word quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta giorni—literally 40 days—the isolation period for ships during plague-era Venice. Should I rabbit-hole research a Venice trip...?

For me, the 40 days/40 nights was a hyper-frantic, self-quarantined final push to the deadline. At the end, I died fully dead. I did not rise again three days later. It took a few weeks.

But I buried the lead—the deadline! I hit it! Please clap!

The draft is done. Eyelid Twitch lingers. It's called eyelid myokymia, by the way: a mild, involuntary spasm of the upper eyelid muscle. It typically resolves on its own, unlike the brain aneurysm I had naturally presumed it was.

* * *

My new book is called ASAP (As SLOW As Possible): When to Take the Long Road in a Shortcut World.

What's it about?

**************************
#176: We're Okay, Actually
**************************

Where I've landed on AI

"AI isn't replacing PMM, it's redefining it."

That's what Elliott Rayner said during his talk on storytelling at the PMM Summit in Amsterdam this week. And, as usual, I think he hit on something really important.

It's been a heavy few weeks (let's be real, months) on the internet recently. But, I feel like we've reached a tipping point.

Last week, Elena Verna and Lenny Rachitsky, two well-known creators in the product and growth space, both sent an email with the same subject line: "You'll lose your job in 2027." The pushback ( https://2699bf44.click.kit-mail3. ) from their audiences on LinkedIn, Twitter and Reddit was almost instant. Elena later apologized and acknowledged the subject line was too aggressive, but it's a sign of the changing times.

People are starting to push back against AI en masse, and the data backs it up.

An April 2026 Gallup study ( https://2699bf44.click.kit-mail3.com/qdu7o0r753f7h4m23g2flh8gvw440h33m2786n952oogd3w227mwldlk9lg7gpk8evn5rln7wvlrm03rx55lwv7r89g48xv89p0px5q8d6mx5ezm7emwede3wvdu83dd7/08hwhgu25z5vxmip/aHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzLmdhbGx1cC5jb20vcG9sbC83MDgyMjQvZ2VuLWFkb3B0aW9uLXN0ZWFkeS1za2VwdGljaXNtLWNsaW1icy5hc3B4 ) found that sentiment toward AI has gotten more negative over the past year, even among the people using it most. Specifically, "Gen Zers’ strong agreement or agreement that they feel excited about AI has dropped 14 percentage points to 22%, while hopefulness has fallen nine points to 18%, and anger has increased nine points to 31%."

Trust is at risk because of this. Klaviyo's 2026 AI Consumer Trends Report ( https://2699bf44.click.kit-mail3.com/qdu7o0r753f7h4m23g2flh8gvw440h33m2786n952oogd3w227mwldlk9lg7gpk8evn5rln7wvlrm03rx55lwv7r89g48xv89p0px5q8d6mx5ezm7emwede3wvdu83dd7/8ghqh3uov9vz3lcl/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cua2xhdml5by5jb20vc29sdXRpb25zL2FpL2NvbnN1bWVyLXRydXN0LWluLWFp ) found that when people think content was made by AI, they're 4 times more likely to trust the brand behind it less. That's a massive risk considering almost every brand I encounter these days seems to be using AI for their marketing.

There's even a name for this now. State of Brand published a great piece this week ( https://2699bf44.click.kit-mail3.com/qdu7o0r753f7h4m23g2flh8gvw440h33m2786n952oogd3w227mwldlk9lg7gpk8evn5rln7wvlrm03rx55lwv7r89g48xv89p0px5q8d6mx5ezm7emwede3wvdu83dd7/vqh3hmuo7g7l4osw/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cudGhlc3RhdGVvZmJyYW5kLmNvbS9uZXdzL3RoZS1ncmVhdC1haS1icmFuZC1mbGF0dGVuaW5n ) on what they've coined the great flattening. Their argument is that AI is making every business sound the same (yeah, we've noticed). That sameness is what makes AI content so easy to spot, and spotting it is what's eroding trust.

People are more hesitant about AI, they trust it less when they see it, and yet the tools themselves are pushing everyone towards the same voice that makes it a dead giveaway. It's one big loop.

That's where we find ourselves today. We cannot ignore what is happening around us but, equally, it is not helpful to play into the fear either.

I want to do something a little different in this week's newsletter. I want to take this opportunity to share my perspective on this conversation.

I'll be honest, I am super anxious about all of this. It's hard not to be. The rate of change feels impossible to keep up with, and I find myself on a fragile line between feeling emotionally exhausted and creatively excited. The future of an industry I've built my career (and in some ways, identity) on is shifting under our feet.

If you feel some version of this yourself, you are not alone. Here's the story I think a lot of us are telling ourselves right now.

Everyone else has figured it out. They've automated their whole workflow and job. They've trained AI to sound exactly like them. They've got a dozen agents running in the background. And you are the one who is getting left behind.

I'm lucky to spend a good part of my week talking directly to product marketers. And the majority of conversations I have in private do not reflect the full panic I often see online. What I actually see is a very wide range of experiences.

Some people are still fighting just to get Claude approved at work. Some are dipping a toe into Cowork and scheduling autonomous tasks. Others have dived right into Claude Code and are building their own PMM tooling from scratch. I've talked to people who've built entire context management systems in Obsidian, and people who are getting by with a couple of markdown files. Everyone is figuring it out at their own pace.

The thing about LinkedIn is that it amplifies the voices of early adopters. There's always a pack leading the way with any new technology, and they are the people who are loudest, fastest, and most excited. Their "volume" makes everyone behind them feel like they're failing. But being behind the earliest of adopters isn't the same as being behind.

You're probably more on track than you think you are.

So no, I don't think everyone is a super user and you're the only one behind. I don't think you will lose your job in 2027. And I also don't think it's responsible to hope this is a hype cycle that will end soon. AI is going to be a meaningful part of how we work moving forward, and I don't really think that's up for debate anymore.

The question is what we do with that. This is where I keep noodling on what Elliott said. AI isn't replacing PMM, it's redefining it. I don't think most of us are about to be replaced any time soon. But I do think the craft of product marketing is being redefined, and the real opportunity right now is to be the ones doing the redefining, rather than waiting to be told what the job becomes.

So how do we redefine it in a way that protects the craft and sets us up for what's next?

I think it starts with being honest about what the craft actually is. At its heart, we're storytellers, and storytelling is artisanal. It's about knowing your audience, capturing attention, creating emotion, and driving behavioural change. ---------------------------------------------------
I was mid-sentence when the client raised his hand.
---------------------------------------------------

“Sorry to cut you off,” he said, “I’m just noticing something—”

I stopped talking and leaned into the screen.

“—looks like you replaced a lot of exclamation marks with periods?”

I nodded and leaned back. “Yeah, I think I removed all of them, actually,” I said. “I was gonna suggest replacing them with periods.”

“All of them?” he said, his tone incredulous. “I’m not arguing, by the way.” He showed me his palms. “I did hire you to edit this thing.” He took a beat. “I’m just curious because I liked them, you know? I thought they created energy?”

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
“The most powerful element in advertising,” said creative director Bill Bernbach, “is truth.”
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

And exclamation marks are, very often, less “truth” and more contrived enthusiasm, hype. And, very often, The Reader sniffs this out, resenting the manipulation.

----------
Years ago:
----------

A direct marketer named Michael Senoff did a fantastic interview with copywriter Ben Settle.

“One question people ask,” Michael said, “is how can you avoid sounding too ‘hype’ in your copy without losing the impact of the big promise, of the benefits?”

Ben didn’t hesitate.

“One way to do this really, really fast,” he said, “is just to either get rid of all the exclamation marks or use them really sparingly. That alone will kind of take away that ‘hype’ feeling, especially if what you’re saying is true, which it should be anyway. If you’re saying something that someone really needs to hear, it doesn’t really matter how you say it, so much as just saying it,” said Ben. “Just saying it alone makes it exciting.”

---------------------------------------
Truth is the ultimate exclamation mark.
---------------------------------------

Put something truly valuable, truly beneficial in front of the ideal prospect, the ideal market, and you won’t need to shout to make it compelling. Just saying it—with a period—makes it exciting.

-------------------------------
I leaned into the screen again.
-------------------------------

“Honestly,” I said, “it’s a great question and thank you for asking it.”

The client nodded. “Really, I’m just curious,” he said. “I’m sure there’s a reason.”

I sipped my coffee. “So,” I said, “have you heard of Bill Bernbach?”

And "we're still experimenting" isn't going to cut it in Q4. So here are 5.5 tips that might help you: Tip 1️⃣: Fix the workflow before you touch the tool. AI on a broken process is just a faster broken process. That's it. Before buying anything, ask: is this workflow actually good? Are there approvals that exist for no reason? Handoffs nobody can explain? Fix those first. Then automate. The order of operations matters more than the tool. Tip 2️⃣: Build a measurement layer on day one. Not day 90. Pick 2 numbers before you turn anything on. Time saved per task. Output volume. Campaign performance. Something real. Tip 3️⃣: Build vs. buy is now actually a real question. 2 years ago this was easy. Problem exists, find vendor, swipe card. Now you can build internal tools in days that used to take quarters. The rule: build when it's specific to how YOUR team works. Buy when you need governance, security, or someone else to have already solved the hard stuff at enterprise scale. Both are right. Doing only 1 of them is expensive. Tip 4️⃣: Your 1st-party data is the moat. Everyone has the same AI tools now. Which means the output is starting to look the same. ## @benradack
What to do when your cost cap campaign stops spending.

When a cost cap campaign slows down or stops spending, it usually means Meta determined it can't find a customer at your set cost cap with the ads, offer, and product you're running.

Here's how I diagnose it step by step.

**1. Test if it's the ads**

→ Turn on an old ad that used to get a lot of spend
→ If it starts spending, your current creative was the problem

**2. Test if it's the offer**

→ If the old ad doesn't fix it, I assume competitors have a better offer
→ Look at what competitors are running and try to match or beat it

**3. Consider the product**

→ If the offer change doesn't work, the issue might be the product itself
→ But you can't change the product easily, so first you have to rule out a broken campaign

**4. Test if the campaign is broken**

→ Duplicate the cost cap campaign so you don't disturb the original
→ Turn the original off
→ Switch the duplicate to highest volume (max conversions)
→ If the highest volume version performs horribly too, something else is going on
→ If it works, your cost cap campaign was just broken

Sometimes a cost cap campaign just dies for no clear reason. Duplicating and switching to highest volume is the cleanest way to figure out if it's the strategy or the campaign itself.

## @benradack
Here's how I set up my promo campaigns.

Single CBO campaign.

→ 1 ad set targeting engaged audiences
→ That means website visitors, add to carts, and past purchasers
→ Make sure audience suggestions are turned ON

With audience suggestions on, Meta looks at your audience selections first, then goes broad from there.

This is the opposite of how I set up prospecting. For promos you want to hit your warm audience hard because they already know the brand. A discount or limited time offer is often all it takes to convert someone who was already considering you.

Promos work best when you include your active customer base. They're the most likely to jump on a deal.

Keep this as its own campaign so when the sale ends you have a clean off switch. Don't mix promo creative into your evergreen campaigns.

Inherited an account last year doing 600k/month. Profitable. The founder thought he'd cracked it.

I asked one question: "Which ad is driving this?"

He didn't know. Neither did his last agency.

They'd been scaling blind for 9 months. One ad — a UGC video a freelancer made for $80 — was carrying 70% of revenue. Everything else was just noise riding its coattails.

Then it fatigued.

Revenue fell off a cliff in 3 weeks.

They didn't have a scaling problem. They had a "we got lucky once and called it a system" problem.

Winning without knowing why is just losing on a delay.

## @lifeofbi
Beyond Meat peaked at $230+ a share in 2019. Today it trades under $1. $13B+ valuation effectively wiped out. 

One of the most dramatic value destruction stories in consumer brand history.

And it happened while the wellness movement was supposed to be the tailwind.

That's the paradox.

Plant-based meat brands built their empire on one thesis: animal protein is bad, engineered plants are better. From 2017 to 2021 it landed perfectly. A Beyond Burger in a Whole Foods basket felt like the future.

Then the anti-UPF revolution happened.

The same MAHA forces driving the seed oil backlash, the tallow revival, and the raw honey trend turned on fake meat with one devastating accusation - it's an industrialised chemistry set.

The health-conscious consumer who went plant-based for longevity in 2019 is the exact same consumer reading ingredient labels in 2026, and rejecting what they used to buy.

Meanwhile mainstream wellness made butter cool again. Grass-fed beef aspirational. Tallow snacks a category. Regenerative agriculture a movement.

So what next for plant-based?

This week I wrote about Brami: lupini bean pasta, two whole ingredients, 400% YoY growth. Last month, fermented vegetables, kimchi and sauerkraut, riding a massive gut health wave.

The vegetarian, vegan, and plant-curious consumer didn't disappear.

Who builds the next clean-label $1B plant-based brand?
